# Larger versus smaller RBC volume per transfusion: original studies available before 2025-08-05

## Executive Summary

Seventeen original studies compare, or plausibly compare, a larger with a smaller red-cell volume per transfusion event; eleven are clearly eligible and six are borderline or less certain. The evidence is not balanced across the three populations.

Preterm and very-low-birth-weight neonates have the most direct trials. Randomised comparisons of 20 versus 15 mL/kg [2][3][4][5] and 20 versus 10 mL/kg [1] each report a higher post-transfusion haemoglobin with the larger volume. In the 10 versus 20 mL/kg trial haemoglobin was 14.2 versus 12.0 g/dL [1], and in the crossover trial 13.2 versus 11.8 g/dL [4]. One trial reported fewer transfusions (1.9 versus 2.6) with 20 mL/kg [5]. A two-unit cohort comparison of 15 versus 20 mL/kg also exists [6].

For children, one large trial applies. The TRACT volume comparison randomised 3196 African children with severe anaemia to 30 versus 20 mL/kg; 28-day mortality was 3.4% in the higher-volume group and 4.5% in the lower-volume group (HR 0.76, 95% CI 0.54 to 1.08) [7]. No other paediatric trial was seen.

For adults, the studies compare one versus two units per transfusion, mostly in haematology and oncology. One randomised trial covers acute leukaemia and transplant [8]; another is a 91-patient factorial pilot in acute myeloid leukaemia [9]. Several before-after or historical-control cohorts accompany them [10][11][12][13]. In the one cohort that reports a figure, the single-unit policy cut RBC use by 32% [11].

Open points: no adult ICU, GI-bleeding, cardiac or obstetric one-versus-two-unit trial was seen; no trial registered on ClinicalTrials.gov was found; and the gateway call ceiling was reached, so the list may be incomplete. Several candidates were judged on title only.

## Introduction

The question asks which original studies (RCTs and non-randomised studies of interventions, NRSIs) compared a larger with a smaller RBC volume per transfusion event, defined as one administration within six hours, in hospitalised adults, children or preterm neonates with anaemia. The date T is 2025-08-05, given explicitly. The plugin used is biology, with PubMed, Europe PMC, OpenAlex, ClinicalTrials.gov and the medRxiv/bioRxiv engines. Reviews were never used as sources; only pointers to study names were allowed.

Method: four parallel searchers covered neonatal, paediatric, adult and registry/terminology angles, then a complement wave and a reading of the possibles from their abstracts. The stop was at the gateway ceiling of 60 calls, not on saturation.

Assumptions. First, "single-unit versus double-unit" policies count as larger versus smaller volume per transfusion event; if only weight-based volume contrasts counted, the adult studies would drop out. Second, liberal versus restrictive threshold trials were excluded unless the volume per transfusion was the compared factor. Third, policy studies of before-after design are kept as NRSIs.

## Main Analysis

### Finding 1 — Neonatal trials consistently show a higher haemoglobin with the larger volume

Randomised trials in preterm infants are the most direct evidence. A trial of birth-weight 500 to 1,500 g infants assigned 10 or 20 mL/kg and found haemoglobin of 14.2 versus 12.0 g/dL after transfusion with 20 mL/kg, with no measured difference in pulmonary function [1]. Wong et al. compared 20 mL/kg with a standard 15 mL/kg in premature infants in a randomised trial [2]. Choi et al. randomised 39 infants born before 34 weeks to 20 versus 15 mL/kg with echocardiographic and BNP safety outcomes [3]. Mallett et al. used a randomised crossover design in 22 stable very-low-birth-weight infants, with haemoglobin of 13.2 versus 11.8 g/dL for 20 versus 15 mL/kg [4]. Chen et al. randomised 73 newborns to 20 mL/kg and 78 to 15 mL/kg and reported 1.9 versus 2.6 transfusions [5].

Qualifications: the trials are small, and the abstracts we read report surrogate outcomes (haemoglobin, haematocrit, number of transfusions, pulmonary or cardiac function) rather than mortality or necrotising enterocolitis. Mallett reported no excess adverse events with the larger volume [4]. Chen's design is labelled an "observational" randomised study in the searcher notes, which makes its design label a point of caution [5]. Von Lindern et al. compared two NICUs transfusing 15 and 20 mL/kg in a cohort and is an NRSI, with the confounding that this implies [6]. Two other candidates were seen on title only: a weight-based versus formula-based dosing trial in preterm neonates [16] and a comparison of transfusion practice in two Dutch neonatal centres [17]; their volume contrasts are not established.

Consequence: for haemoglobin response, the direction is concordant in five randomised studies. Verdict: established for the haemoglobin outcome, open for clinical outcomes and safety.

### Finding 2 — In children, TRACT is the only trial of volume, and it was inconclusive for mortality

The TRACT trial was a factorial, open-label trial randomising African children with severe anaemia (haemoglobin below 6 g/dL) to 20 or 30 mL/kg. In 3196 children, 28-day mortality was 3.4% in the higher-volume group and 4.5% in the lower-volume group, with HR 0.76 (95% CI 0.54 to 1.08) and heterogeneity by fever [7]. The searches did not reveal a paediatric trial of 10 versus 20 mL/kg, nor a paediatric sickle-cell or oncology volume trial. TRACT's secondary analyses addressed pack type or sickle-cell and malaria subgroups and did not compare volume, so they were excluded.

Qualification: TRACT is a single cluster of evidence, in a low-resource African setting with a high malaria burden, so transfer to other hospitalised children is indirect. Consequence: one large trial, with an interval that includes no effect. Verdict: open for children outside this setting.

### Finding 3 — Adult evidence is two small randomised trials on single versus double units, in haematology

Chantepie et al. randomised patients with acute leukaemia or transplant on a haematological ICU to a single RBC or a double RBC per transfusion [8]. Byun et al. ran a pilot 2x2 factorial in 91 patients with acute myeloid leukaemia on chemotherapy, combining a haemoglobin trigger of 7 versus 8 g/dL with single versus double units; units per transfusion did not change total RBC use, outcomes or bleeding as summarised from the abstract [9].

Qualifications: both are in haematological malignancy; Byun is a pilot [9]. No randomised trial in general medical, surgical, ICU or GI-bleeding populations was found. Consequence: the randomised adult evidence is narrow. Verdict: probable that unit number per transfusion has little effect on clinical outcomes in this population, with low certainty.

### Finding 4 — Adult before-after and historical cohorts show fewer units used under single-unit policies

Bowman et al. compared malignant haematology patients before and after a single-unit policy, with fewer units per admission but more transfusion episodes and a lower discharge haemoglobin, and no difference in length of stay or 30-day mortality [10]. Marco-Ayala et al. compared 187 patients under a single-unit policy with 153 historical double-unit patients in autologous stem-cell transplant; RBC use fell 32%, and length of stay, discharge haemoglobin and 30-day mortality did not differ [11]. Heyes et al. reported six months before and after a single-unit policy on eight general medical wards, with single-unit orders rising from 30% to 53% [12]. Berger et al. studied a change from double-unit to single-unit policy in patients on intensive chemotherapy or transplant (title only) [13]. Ma et al. retrospectively analysed adults given one or two units, estimating the one-unit effect by dividing the haemoglobin change by two [14], and Bosch et al. described a haemoglobin-triggered single-unit policy for haemato-oncology inpatients, assessed on title only [15].

Qualifications: these are before-after or historical designs exposed to temporal confounding, and Ma's modelled contrast is not a direct comparison [14]. Consequence: they support unit sparing without evident harm on short-term outcomes. Verdict: probable for haematology, open elsewhere.

## Synthesis & Insights

Our analysis: the evidence splits by population. Neonates have weight-based volume trials with concordant haemoglobin gains, children have a single large trial, and adults have unit-count contrasts that are mostly policy changes. The outcomes differ as well: neonatal studies measure haemoglobin, whereas adult studies measure RBC use and clinical outcomes, so the larger-volume question is answered for different endpoints. Safety evidence for larger volumes is thin everywhere, with only short-term cardiopulmonary measures [1][3][4].

## Limitations & Caveats

The gateway ceiling of 60 calls was reached, so completeness is not guaranteed. Searches did not surface any registered trial in ClinicalTrials.gov, and PubMed and OpenAlex handled long Boolean queries poorly. Several candidates were judged on title only [13][15][16][17]. Fewer than twenty sources carry the report. Cardiac, obstetric and ICU single-unit studies were searched without result; studies comparing single-unit patients with untransfused patients were excluded as not comparing volumes.

## Recommendations

Treat the list as the core set and verify the borderline entries against full texts. Search further for adult single versus double unit trials outside haematology, for neonatal and paediatric trials with clinical outcomes, and for trial registrations in registries other than ClinicalTrials.gov.

## Methodology Appendix

Process: 4 searchers in wave 1 (48 calls, about 14 eligible studies), then a complement searcher plus an abstract reader in wave 2 (13 calls; new eligible: Paul 2002 and Berger 2012, plus two borderline). Stopping rule: gateway ceiling reached, not saturation. Plan revision: findings regrouped by population; under half of the plan changed.

Source coverage: active: PubMed, Europe PMC, OpenAlex, ClinicalTrials.gov, medRxiv/bioRxiv, Crossref. Skipped: none announced. Suggestions: none.

Verification: rule "verified = what carries a decision"; sentences of the findings not in the executive summary or a verdict are not checked (traceable by [n]). 12 claims checked: 11 FOUND, 1 DISTORTED, 0 ABSENT, 0 INVALID, 0 unverified, no removals. DISTORTED corrected from the discrepancy, not re-verified: [7] (arm assignment of the 3.4% and 4.5% mortality figures, now stated as higher-volume versus lower-volume group). Claims kept unverified: none.

Plugin biases looked for: indirectness (population, surrogate outcomes), confounding in before-after designs, preprint status (none found), publication bias (registry search found nothing). Cost: about 59 gateway calls plus 5 searchers/reader sub-agents. Mode: standard. Machine annex: card.json, result.json.

Summary: seventeen studies compare larger with smaller RBC volume per transfusion, mostly neonatal 20 versus 15 mL/kg trials, TRACT in children, and single versus double unit studies in adult haematology.
